sections.relationship: Students miscount neighbors on a busy map. Turning each region into a dot and each shared border into a line gives a small graph that is easy to count and color.
sections.author_note: Students miscount neighbors on a busy map. Turning each region into a dot and each shared border into a line gives a small graph that is easy to count and color.

lesson.title: Draw the neighbor graph
text: Put one dot for each region.
Walk around each region's border and draw a line to every region it shares a border with. A corner touch is not a border.
The number of lines at a dot is the number of neighbors.
To color the map, color the dots so that every line joins two different colors. Start with the region that has the most neighbors.

example.title: Worked example (a different map)
prompt: Four regions W, X, Y, Z: W borders X and Y; X borders Y and Z; Y borders Z.
steps: Lines: W-X, W-Y, X-Y, X-Z, Y-Z.
W, X, Y all border each other, so they need 3 different colors: W red, X blue, Y green.
Z borders X and Y, so Z must be red. Three colors are enough.

questions.prompt: Some map drawn on a page needs at least 4 colors so that neighbors differ.

A map has regions in a ring: region 1 borders 2, 2 borders 3, and so on, and the last region borders region 1 (and there are no other borders). Give a number of regions n, from 3 to 10, for which 2 colors are NOT enough.
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: isOdd(n) and n >= 3 and n <= 10 (example: n = 5)
